posts.title: What is ADHD?
posts.hook: ADHD is a recognised neurodevelopmental condition described by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity with functional impact.
posts.author: MJB ADHD
body: ADHD is a recognised neurodevelopmental condition described by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity with functional impact.

ADHD is a recognised neurodevelopmental condition described by persistent patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity with functional impact. The outward pattern can differ across people, settings and life stages.

slides.heading: What genes can and cannot tell you
slides.body: There is no single “ADHD gene”. The picture is thousands of common variants that each nudge risk a tiny amount, plus rarer variants with bigger effects, plus chance and environment (Tier B). Genes describe risk. They are not a diagnostic test and they do not tell a clinician which medication to use (Tier B).

body: This is a map of how one dopamine-releasing nerve cell in the brain makes, stores and releases dopamine, and of what then happens to the dopamine.

This is a map of how one dopamine-releasing nerve cell in the brain makes, stores and releases dopamine, and of what then happens to the dopamine. The biology of each step is well established (Tier A). Whether a weak step explains ADHD in any particular person is an open question (Tier D), and the map does not answer it.

slides.heading: Main line: inside a brain dopamine cell
slides.body: Tyrosine in the blood is carried into the brain by LAT1. Tyrosine hydroxylase needs BH4 to work. Tyrosine hydroxylase's product, L-DOPA, is converted to dopamine by AADC. Newly made dopamine is loaded into vesicles by VMAT2. Filled vesicles release dopamine when calcium enters the nerve ending.

slides.body: Methylphenidate mainly inhibits the dopamine and noradrenaline transporters. Amphetamine also inhibits them, can make them run in reverse, and inhibits VMAT2.
